case: A fictional vehicle-repair workshop: profitable over the year, but deciding whether it can safely release cash today.
caseLabel: Fictional workshop • annual earnings and dated cash are separate tests
units: NI — after-tax, after-interest net income; KES/year
D&A — depreciation and amortisation; noncash expense
Maintenance — spending needed to preserve current service
ΔNWC — increase in required operating working capital
Headroom — dated available cash less obligations and reserve

beats.title: Profit is the starting point
points: KES 1.8m net income describes a reported period.
Add back KES 240,000 of supported noncash charges.
Deduct the KES 300,000 shortfall between current owner pay and replacement labour.
beats.notes: Part 1 workshop and Appendix 01 A1.1–A1.2. Only the replacement-pay shortfall is adjusted; do not subtract the full replacement salary a second time.

beats.title: Keep today’s service intact
points: Deduct KES 380,000 maintenance investment.
Deduct KES 370,000 increased required working capital.
The KES 300,000 second-bay expansion is a separate growth use.
beats.notes: Article Case C5:F18. The historical cash-after-total-capex proxy also equals KES 990,000 in this case. Explain that this numerical equality is coincidental; the definitions differ.

beats.title: A cash draw must meet dated claims
points: Bank cash of KES 1.2m faces KES 910,000 listed uses.
A KES 150,000 reserve leaves KES 140,000 provisional headroom.
Removing a disputed KES 200,000 receipt leaves a KES 60,000 deficit.
beats.notes: Article Case C21:F33. The disputed amount was mistakenly counted in available cash; remove it once. This liquidity screen does not establish a legal distribution entitlement.

calculation.title: The annual owner-earnings bridge
calculation.equation: OE = NI + D&A − maintenance − ΔNWC − pay shortfall
calculation.interpretation: The result estimates normalized annual earning power before separate growth spending, debt principal and reserve choices.
calculation.notes: Fictional Article Case. Keep the separate general Owner Earnings worksheet's KES 2.2m scenario out of this calculation.

scenario.title: Test the proposed KES 30,000 withdrawal
scenario.changed: Deduct a proposed KES 30,000 owner withdrawal.
scenario.consequence: Dated headroom becomes KES −90,000; annual owner earnings remains KES 990,000.
scenario.notes: Scenario from the free-calculator reconciliation map. Hold all other dated inputs fixed. A profitable year cannot fund a payment before cash arrives.

answer: Normalized owner earnings and cash available today answer different questions. The workshop earns KES 990,000 on the annual bridge, yet its reviewed dated cash test is already KES 60,000 short.
action: Prepare one matched earnings bridge and one dated obligations list. Reconcile disputed receipts before approving a draw.

case: A fictional small business tests whether asset replacement and seasonal working capital are consuming cash needed to maintain service.
caseLabel: Fictional maintenance register and October–December snapshots
units: DSO — receivables ÷ matched credit sales × period days
DIO — inventory ÷ matched cost of sales × period days
DPO — payables ÷ matched credit purchases × period days
CCC — DIO + DSO − DPO; days
NWC — receivables + inventory − payables; KES

beats.title: Depreciation is not a replacement quote
points: Start with the service an asset provides and the cost of failure.
Separate renewal that preserves capacity from a project that adds capacity.
Replace placeholder compressor and van costs with dated quotes and inspections.
beats.notes: Part 2; Maintenance C5:I12; Appendix 02. Accounting depreciation allocates historical cost and need not equal current renewal cash.

beats.title: Match every operating-cycle denominator
points: Use credit sales for DSO and credit purchases for DPO.
Keep balance dates and the denominator period explicit.
Discuss average balances and seasonality before generalising from a month-end snapshot.
beats.notes: Working Capital C5:O8. The corrected sheet uses receivables/credit sales, inventory/cost of sales and payables/credit purchases.

beats.title: A shorter cycle can hide weaker service
points: Reducing stock can release cash but cause stock-outs.
A longer payable period may be overdue debt rather than negotiated credit.
Track disputes, customer advances and aged items alongside the day ratios.
beats.notes: Receivables, Inventory and Payables sheets; Part 2 practical data request. A ratio is diagnostic and is not a target independent of service conditions.

calculation.title: Make the cash-conversion cycle visible
calculation.interpretation: The cycle describes a timing relationship. NWC separately measures the cash amount tied up in the matched operating balances.
calculation.notes: Fictional workbook Working Capital J6:N8. Ratios shown at the workbook's displayed precision.

scenario.title: Seasonal growth ties up another KES 0.9m
scenario.consequence: The snapshots show KES 900,000 more working capital and a 10-day longer cycle. Investigate sales mix, stock and collections before choosing an action.
scenario.notes: This is a comparison of fictional workbook months, not a controlled one-input sensitivity. Read the underlying balances and denominators before attributing causation.

answer: Cash required to preserve service includes replacement assets and operating-cycle investment. Matched balances and periods make those requirements visible; the cash schedule determines when they must be funded.
action: Create a replacement register and a seasonal working-capital record with source dates, quote owners and unresolved evidence.

case: A weekly operating meeting identifies the earliest cash shortfall, the invoice behind it and the person responsible for the next action.
units: Opening cash — available cash at the start of the week; KES
Receipts — expected collections, distinct from invoice revenue
Contribution — price less variable product and fulfilment costs
Reserve breach — closing cash below the chosen reserve
Shortfall — closing cash below zero; funding remains explicit

beats.title: Read the week as a cash story
points: Start with opening cash and evidence-backed receipt dates.
Deduct suppliers, payroll, fixed costs and other due claims.
Carry a negative balance forward; do not silently insert rescue borrowing.
beats.notes: Cash13W C5:N25 and Overview D4. Source cases are fictional. A weekly model does not prove that each payment clears within that week.

beats.title: Turn exceptions into operating work
points: For receivables, distinguish due date, dispute status and expected collection.
For stock, use last-sale date, lead time and safety stock.
For suppliers, record contractual due date and operational criticality.
beats.notes: Receivables C5:N27, Inventory C5:Q19, Payables C5:N19. The sample SKUs and counterparties are teaching records.

beats.title: Contribution must fund more than the product
points: Price less product and fulfilment cost gives contribution per unit.
Volume turns unit contribution into monthly contribution.
Fixed costs, tax, finance and owner needs remain outside that unit margin.
beats.notes: Unit Economics C5:L7. Contribution is not net income. Explain the cost behaviour before interpreting a break-even quantity.

calculation.title: Follow each closing cash balance
calculation.equation: Closing cash = opening cash + receipts + financing − cash uses
calculation.substitution: Base case: minimum cash KES 1.05m; final cash KES 1.95m
calculation.interpretation: The lowest cash week is the action point. A positive final week can conceal an earlier reserve breach.
calculation.notes: Cash13W rows 6:18; free-calculator reconciliation map verifies all thirteen baseline closing balances. Financing receipts are separate from customer collections.

scenario.title: The downside needs action before week 3
scenario.baseline: Base minimum KES 1.05m; final cash KES 1.95m.
scenario.changed: Select the source downside receipts and uses.
scenario.consequence: Reserve breach starts in week 2; cash turns negative in week 3; final cash is KES −6.65m.
scenario.notes: This is the workbook's multi-input downside, not a one-variable forecast. The web tool can separately delay receipts one week; amounts arriving after week 13 must be disclosed.

answer: An operating dashboard is useful when a cash or service exception produces a named action before the trough. The invoice, stock or supplier record explains the mechanism behind the weekly total.
action: Write one action with an owner, due date, evidence trigger and expected cash or service effect.

case: An owner considers a draw, a reserve, new capacity and a loan while protecting payroll and supplier payments.
caseLabel: Fictional financing options • terms are not lender offers or APRs
units: Tenor — time until the facility must be repaid
Principal — borrowed balance before interest and fees
Reserve — cash assigned to a named risk
Growth investment — cash to add capacity or capability
Repayment source — dated operating receipt or other documented source

beats.title: Assign each use a funding horizon
points: A multi-year asset and a short receivable gap need different facilities.
Supplier credit needs written terms and a payment date.
A reserve should name the risk and conditions for release or replenishment.
beats.notes: Part 4 reserve framework and Debt and Growth C5:J14. Start with the cash use, rather than selecting a loan from its rate alone.

beats.title: Read the three illustrative offers
points: Term facility: KES 5m, 16% annual rate and 2% fee.
Revolver: KES 3m, 19% annual rate and 1.5% fee.
Supplier credit: KES 1.5m at 8% for a quarter.
beats.notes: Debt and Growth C5:J9. Different tenors and fee conventions prevent these headline rates from being an all-in APR ranking.

beats.title: Growth must produce a collection path
points: Trace verified demand into contribution and operating cash.
Include extra stock, receivables and delayed collections.
Set a stop condition before committing the next tranche.
beats.notes: Debt and Growth C11:E14, Cash13W and Unit Economics. A profit forecast alone is not a dated repayment source.

calculation.title: Separate earning power from available cash
calculation.equation: Available cash = opening cash + collected receipts − dated uses
calculation.substitution: A loan adds cash at draw and creates later interest, fees and principal obligations.
calculation.interpretation: Match the facility to the trough and show the repayment source before its contractual due date.
calculation.notes: Use Cash13W for timing. The general Owner Earnings bridge and Article Case are distinct scenarios and are not combined here.

scenario.title: A collection delay can break the repayment case
scenario.baseline: Plan repayment against the documented collection date.
scenario.changed: Move that receipt beyond the debt due date; hold the contract unchanged.
scenario.consequence: The cash gap grows even if annual profit is unchanged. Revise the operating plan or obtain an explicit financing amendment.
scenario.notes: Conceptual timing sensitivity from Part 4; quantify using the viewer's dated facility and receipt. Do not assume automatic rollover or invent late-payment charges.

answer: Draws, reserves, growth and debt compete for dated cash. A sound decision makes the use, timing, repayment source and downside response explicit.
action: Complete a financing decision record: cash use, source of repayment, downside action, decision owner and review date.

case: A buyer tests which earnings, customer relationships and operating responsibilities will transfer when the owner leaves.
caseLabel: Diligence and succession exercise • no sale-price estimate
units: Transferable earnings — earnings after replacing owner-dependent work
Add-back — proposed adjustment requiring documentary support
Normal NWC — operating balance needed at handover; KES
Cost to complete — cash required to satisfy inherited commitments
30/60/90 plan — staged transition milestones and named owners

beats.title: The buyer acquires an operating system
points: Identify assets, contracts and permissions that legally transfer.
Name customer and supplier relationships dependent on the owner.
Separate the business's obligations from the seller's personal arrangements.
beats.notes: Part 5; Buy Sell and Succession C5:H13. A headline profit or negotiated multiple does not establish what changes hands.

beats.title: Rebuild earnings after the owner leaves
points: Cost replacement labour for the duties that continue.
Include maintenance and normalized seasonal working capital.
Keep unsupported add-backs visibly unresolved.
beats.notes: Owner Earnings and Article Case; Appendix 03. Never merge the two workbook scenarios. Trace revenue to invoices and bank receipts.

beats.title: Continuity becomes measurable at handover
points: Confirm title, contracts, taxes, creditor claims and stock condition.
Assign a successor to each critical operating task.
Review customer retention, delivery errors and collections at 30, 60 and 90 days.
beats.notes: Buy Sell and Succession rows 6–13. Link succession measures to actual service commitments and counterparty approvals.

calculation.title: Transferable cash is an evidence bridge
calculation.equation: Transferable earnings = reported earnings ± supported adjustments
calculation.substitution: Adjust replacement labour, maintenance and normal working-capital needs before considering a price.
calculation.interpretation: A cash-capacity estimate is an input to diligence; it is not a negotiated enterprise or equity value.
calculation.notes: Part 5 and Appendix 03. Review debt, surplus assets, contingent claims and deal structure separately before moving from enterprise value to equity consideration.

scenario.title: Replace the founder before trusting the margin
scenario.baseline: The owner handles quotations, approvals and key-customer relationships.
scenario.changed: Cost a successor and test contract consent and customer retention.
scenario.consequence: Transferable earnings can fall and continuity risk can remain even when historical accounts are accurate.
scenario.notes: Qualitative diligence scenario; do not invent a replacement salary or retention percentage. Obtain role-specific evidence and then update the cash bridge.

answer: Earnings become transferable only when the people, permissions, customers, assets and cash obligations needed to produce them survive the transaction. Unresolved transfer conditions belong in the diligence record.
action: Produce a diligence file and 30/60/90-day transition plan with a named successor for each critical duty.
